The Provo regression specifies a straight-line conditional mean. We now need an estimation rule. **Ordinary least squares (OLS)** chooses the coefficients whose fitted values minimize the residual sum of squares.

## From discrepancies to an objective

For position $i$,

$$
\widehat y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i
$$

and

$$
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

The OLS objective is

$$
\operatorname{SSE}(\beta_0,\beta_1)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\right)^2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to the coefficients and setting both derivatives to zero gives

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2}
$$

and

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\overline y-\widehat\beta_1\overline x.
$$

## Computing the Provo regression estimate

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-ols-by-hand
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
x <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
x_bar <- mean(x)
y_bar <- mean(y)

slope_by_hand <-
  sum((x - x_bar) * (y - y_bar)) /
  sum((x - x_bar)^2)
intercept_by_hand <- y_bar - slope_by_hand * x_bar

fit <- lm(y ~ x)

stopifnot(
  abs(slope_by_hand - coef(fit)[["x"]]) < 1e-12,
  abs(intercept_by_hand - coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]]) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  term = c("intercept", "modeled cloze surprisal"),
  estimate_by_hand = c(intercept_by_hand, slope_by_hand),
  estimate_from_lm = unname(coef(fit))
)
```

The fitted slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_by_hand)` log milliseconds per bit. Squaring makes large vertical discrepancies count more heavily, which is one reason a few unusual responses may affect the fit.

If

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2),
$$

then the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
=
-n\log\sigma
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2
+C.
$$

For fixed $\sigma$, maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing SSE. OLS and Gaussian maximum likelihood thus select the same coefficient estimates.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-ols-fit
#| fig-cap: "Reader-aggregated Provo positions and the OLS conditional mean."
plot_data <- transform(provo, cloze_surprisal_bits = x)
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 160L)
)
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = grid$cloze_surprisal_bits))

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(plot_data, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first-fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

OLS estimates the best line under its squared-error criterion. It does not establish that the line is an adequate description, nor does it account for the passage grouping. Those questions require uncertainty calculations and diagnostics.

## Check your understanding

1. Which quantity does OLS minimize?
2. Why does the slope contain cross-products of centered $x$ and $y$?
3. Under which response model does OLS coincide with maximum likelihood?
4. What feature of squared error makes influence worth checking later?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. OLS minimizes the residual sum of squares, $\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The centered cross-products measure whether deviations in $x$ and $y$ have the same direction; dividing by centered $x$ variation converts that co-movement into change in $y$ per unit $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. OLS coefficient estimates coincide with maximum likelihood under independent normal responses with linear means and a common variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Squaring gives unusually large residuals disproportionate weight, so a few observations can strongly affect the fitted coefficients. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd) derives uncertainty in the fitted slope.
